- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Fabric-based packaging such as cotton or linen is a sustainable alternative.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Mushroom or mycelium packaging made from fungi that can be grown locally is a sustainable option.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Edible packaging made from starch or seaweed, which can be eaten with the product or biodegrade quickly, is a sustainable alternative.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Liquid wood made from biodegradable polymers derived from plant materials is a sustainable option.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Reusable or refillable containers that can be returned to the point of origin for refill, such as tiffin boxes or milk bottles, are sustainable alternatives.
- [USER] User finds edible packaging interesting but is concerned about its ability to hold up against moisture and spills.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Edible packaging is still in its early stages of development, and manufacturers are working on materials that can withstand moisture and spills.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some edible packaging materials are coated with a layer of wax or plant-based oil for protection.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some edible packaging is made from starch-based materials that are water-resistant.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Edible packaging is most suitable for dry or semi-dry goods, such as snacks or confectionery products.
- [USER] User is concerned that edible packaging may add extra cost to the product and does not want to pay more for packaging.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Edible packaging currently has a higher cost than plastic packaging due to more expensive materials and complex processing.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Companies are working to optimize production processes and reduce costs for edible packaging.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] While edible packaging may have extra costs upfront, it supports long-term sustainability goals and can ultimately save costs over time.
